idiom_name: #private fields (hard private at runtime) with one mediating method; Proxy traps where interception is required
implementation_notes: TypeScript inherits JavaScript's hard privacy when it is used: #-prefixed fields remain private after compilation and do not offer the escape hatches of the type-level keyword, so they are the only class element form that can carry a mediator's state, and the public methods become the single route in. The compiler's own private keyword is a type annotation only - the handbook shows it is escapable through bracket notation and casts - so it documents intent without enforcing anything at runtime. Where mediation must cover dynamic property access (facades, membranes) a Proxy with get/set traps runs the check on each operation, with the same caveat as JavaScript: hand out the proxy, never the target. Framework guards at the HTTP edge provide the always-invoked property for requests, which is a separate layer from the object-level mediator and does not replace it.
pitfalls: The TypeScript private keyword is erased at runtime and escapable with bracket access or as any; only # fields are enforced by the engine.
When compiling to ES2021 or earlier, TypeScript emits WeakMaps in place of #: behaviour stays private, but the mediator's state becomes an external map, which changes debugging and serialization.
A Proxy does not forward private fields and callers holding the raw target bypass the traps; only the proxy may be handed out.
Returning a mutable object or array from the mediator leaves an unmediated reference with the caller; return copies or frozen views.
